topic: Default `std::async` Policy Allows Synchronous Deferred Execution
explanation: Assumption: Calling `std::async(f)` guarantees that the function `f` will execute concurrently on a separate thread immediately or shortly after the call. Reality: `std::async` uses the default launch policy `std::launch::async | std::launch::deferred`. This policy permits the implementation to defer execution until the resultant `std::future`'s `get()` or `wait()` member function is called. In the deferred case, the function executes synchronously in the thread that waits for the result. Why It Fails: If asynchronous execution is required (e.g., for time-sensitive tasks or UI responsiveness), relying on the default policy is dangerous because execution might be deferred. To guarantee concurrency, the policy must be explicitly specified as `std::launch::async` (e.g., `std::async(std::launch::async, f)`).
practical_example: A program uses `std::async` to launch a long computation, intending to perform other work while waiting. Because the system is under load, the implementation chooses `deferred` execution. When the main thread calls `future.get()`, the entire long computation runs synchronously, freezing the application.
chapter: Item 36: Specify std::launch::async if asynchronous execution is necessary
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
